analysis.one_liner: Requires the president to get Congress's approval to keep new tariffs in place beyond 60 days.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan tariff-review bill has received no committee action since its April 2025 referral, leaving presidential tariff authority unchanged.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require the president to tell Congress within 48 hours whenever a new tariff is imposed or an existing one is raised, including the reasoning and an estimate of how it affects U.S. businesses and consumers. Any such tariff would automatically end after 60 days unless Congress passes a law approving it, and Congress could pass a fast-tracked resolution to end a tariff at any time. Routine trade-remedy duties aimed at dumped or subsidized imports would be exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, consumers and U.S. businesses that pay higher prices because of tariffs would gain the most: every new or increased presidential tariff would come with a written explanation and an assessment of its impact on businesses and consumers within 48 hours, and it would automatically expire after 60 days unless both chambers of Congress affirmatively approved it. Any member of Congress could force a quick up-or-down vote to end a tariff. Exporters and farmers who face retaliation from other countries when U.S. tariffs go up would also benefit if tariffs became shorter-lived.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the president to explain, within 48 hours, why a new or increased tariff was imposed and to estimate its impact on U.S. businesses and consumers.
Sunsets any new or increased tariff after 60 days unless both chambers of Congress enact a joint resolution approving it.
Lets any member of Congress introduce a fast-tracked joint resolution to disapprove a tariff, using expedited procedures that guarantee consideration.
Exempts antidumping and countervailing duties, so established remedies against dumped or subsidized imports are unaffected.

analysis.who_pays: The main "payer" is the presidency itself, which would lose the ability to keep tariffs in place indefinitely without congressional consent. Industries that benefit from tariff protection — and any administration relying on tariffs as bargaining leverage — would also bear costs, since a duty imposed without congressional approval would end after 60 days.
analysis.who_pays_short: Presidential tariff authority and protected industries

drawbacks.text: The enforcement mechanism is weaker than it looks: a joint resolution of disapproval still must be enacted into law, meaning a president who opposes it could veto it, and overriding a veto requires two-thirds of both chambers.

Requiring affirmative congressional approval for tariffs within 60 days could tie the president's hands in trade negotiations, since foreign governments could simply wait out any tariff rather than make concessions.
Even the bill's own terms let either chamber change its rules, so the expedited procedures that guarantee disapproval votes could be altered or dropped by a majority at any time.
The bill was assigned to two committees, including Rules, which adds procedural hurdles before it could ever reach the floor.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: tariffs function as a tax on imports that shows up in consumer prices, and this bill would force each one to be publicly justified and to lapse unless Congress affirmatively agrees. The costs are mostly on the executive side, though an honest case exists that 60-day expirations could weaken the president's bargaining position in trade disputes. The biggest weakness is design rather than cost: because a disapproval resolution must still survive a presidential veto, the bill restrains a cooperative president far more than an uncooperative one.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2025 and sent to two House committees, and nothing has happened since — no hearing, no vote, no movement.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 7, 2025, by Rep. Don Bacon with Reps. Hurd, Gottheimer, and Meeks as original cosponsors.
It was referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee and also to the Rules Committee.
The bill has 8 cosponsors, 3 Republicans and 5 Democrats.
No committee action, markup, or floor vote has occurred since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The current arrangement, in which the president can impose or raise tariffs without a time limit and without congressional approval, remains intact because the bill has not advanced. Import-protected industries and the executive's trade authority are the status quo winners so far; consumers and tariff-exposed businesses have gained nothing yet.

sides.party_line_note: The bill is bipartisan in sponsorship — 8 of 9 supporters are cosponsors, split 3 Republicans and 5 Democrats — but no vote has occurred to reveal how the parties would line up.

industries.note: Tariffs raise the cost of imported goods and inputs, which shows up in retail prices. A 60-day expiration unless Congress approves would limit how long those costs persist.

industries.industry: Industries protected by tariffs (e.g., steel, aluminum)
industries.note: Companies that rely on congressional tariff protection could lose it after 60 days, but antidumping and countervailing duties — the main tools protecting these industries — are explicitly exempted from the bill.
Tariffs invite retaliation against U.S. exports; shorter-lived tariffs would reduce the window for other countries to retaliate against farm goods and manufactured exports.
The bill does not diminish presidential trade power outright — it makes Congress a co-decision-maker, which could entrench tariff policy when both branches agree, while limiting it when they do not.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has had no committee action since its April 2025 referral, and most bills referred to Ways and Means never reach the floor. Tariff-clipping legislation faces additional headwinds: leadership has shown little appetite for constraining current trade policy, and the president could veto any disapproval resolution. Without a scheduled markup or a discharge petition, the realistic path is that the bill stays in committee unless tariff-related economic pain builds enough political pressure to force a vote.
